title: How to answer restaurant wait time questions
description: Answer restaurant wait time questions with clear scripts, realistic timing, and hold strategies that keep callers calm and orders moving.
question: How do I answer the restaurant wait time question on the phone without slowing down the line?
answer: Answer with the truth, a short range, and one clear next step. Say how long pickup, delivery, or a table will likely take, then give the caller the option to order now, place a hold, or leave a name and phone number if the estimate changes.
summary: You’ll know how to give clear wait times, set expectations, and keep phone calls moving during busy service.
intro:
The best answer to the restaurant wait time question is short, honest, and specific. Give a range, not a guess, and say what affects it right now.

If you are slammed, say that plainly and still offer a next step. A good phone host can do that for you, and [ROAL](/facts) can quote a ready time from the live menu and send the order to the kitchen when the caller is ready.

sections.h2: What should I say when someone asks, “How long is the wait?”
sections.body:
Start with the type of wait the caller means. Pickup, delivery, and a table are different questions, so answer the one they asked.

A simple script works well:

> “For pickup right now, we’re about 20 to 25 minutes. If you want, I can take the order now and give you the earliest ready time.”

If the caller means a table, use a different script:

> “We’re about 15 minutes for two, and a little longer for a larger group.”

Use real numbers from your kitchen, not a wish. If your current ticket pile is long, add a buffer. For example, if your usual pickup time is 15 minutes and you have a rush, say 25 to 30 minutes. Plug in your own normal times and your own rush buffer.

sections.h2: How do I give a wait time that feels honest and useful?
sections.body:
A good wait time has three parts: the range, the reason, and the next step. That keeps the caller from hearing a bare number and hanging up.

Try this pattern:

1. State the estimate.
2. Say what is driving it, in plain words.
3. Offer to place the order, reservation, or callback.

Example:

> “We’re running about 30 minutes for pickup because the dinner rush just hit. I can take your order now so it’s in line.”

If you are using ROAL, the host can answer common questions like hours, address, parking, and menu items while also quoting a ready time for orders taken from the live menu. That matters because the caller gets one clear answer instead of being bounced around.

Keep the language simple. Don’t say “maybe soon” or “we’re busy.” Say “25 to 30 minutes” or “about 10 minutes longer than usual.”

sections.h2: What if the caller is upset about the wait?
sections.body:
Do not argue with the caller. Acknowledge the delay, give the reason only if it helps, and offer a choice.

Use a line like this:

> “I hear you. We’re a little backed up right now, and the earliest pickup is 35 minutes. If you want, I can still place it now, or I can take your name and call you back if the timing changes.”

Concrete checklist for a tense call:

- Repeat the wait time once.
- Do not over-explain the kitchen.
- Offer pickup, delivery, or reservation options only if they fit your restaurant.
- Take the caller’s name and phone if you need to update them.
- If the call turns into a complaint, hand it to staff with a summary.

ROAL can hand complaints and manager requests to staff with a summary, which helps when the call stops being a simple “how long is the wait?” question and turns into a service issue.

sections.h2: How can I set different wait times for pickup, delivery, and busy periods?
sections.body:
Make a small wait-time chart for the phone team. Keep it near the register or kitchen screen so the answer stays consistent.

| Situation | What to say |
|---|---|
| Slow hour pickup | “About 10 to 15 minutes.” |
| Normal pickup | “About 20 minutes.” |
| Dinner rush pickup | “About 30 to 40 minutes.” |
| Delivery order | “About 45 minutes, depending on driver availability.” |
| Large order | “It may take a bit longer, so I’ll confirm the ready time when I place it.” |

Use your own numbers. If your kitchen usually needs 18 minutes for a small order and 35 minutes for a large family meal, write those down and tell every caller the same thing.

A short step list helps staff stay aligned:

1. Check the current ticket line.
2. Add your normal prep time.
3. Add a buffer for the rush.
4. Quote the result as a range.
5. Give the caller one next step.

This keeps the answer practical and prevents one person from saying 15 minutes while another says 40.

sections.h2: How does wait time affect phone orders and revenue?
sections.body:
When a caller hears a clear wait time, they can decide faster. That matters because silence or a vague answer often sends them to another place.

Here is a simple example you can swap for your own numbers. Say your average pickup order is $28. If you answer the phone with a clear 25-minute wait, the caller may stay and place the order. If you say, “We’re really busy,” without a time, they may hang up and try somewhere else. The value of a clear answer is not the exact number; it is keeping the caller on the line long enough to order.

Use this checklist during rush periods:

- Know your current wait before you answer the phone.
- Keep a short script ready.
- Stop promising “soon” without a number.
- Route tricky questions to staff.
- Update the kitchen screen if the wait changes.

Some owners use ROAL because it can answer the phone, quote a ready time, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also reads the live menu, so the host can avoid offering sold-out items.

sections.h2: How do I handle wait time questions after hours or when I’m short-staffed?
sections.body:
After hours, the answer should be even simpler. Tell the caller whether you are open, when you reopen, and what they can do next.

Example script:

> “We’re closed right now. We reopen tomorrow at 11. If you want to place a pickup order then, I can note the details once we’re open.”

On a short-staffed shift, keep the answer short and honest:

> “We’re running about 35 minutes for pickup tonight.”

If you want a steadier setup for those moments, [Build a free test host](/try) from your website or Google Maps link and see how a phone host handles the common questions first. The setup is quick, and you can test-call it in the browser before you go live.

Remember the limits. It does not take card numbers over the phone. If a caller has a tricky allergy question, a catering request, or a manager issue, the phone host passes it to staff with a summary. That is often the safest handoff for a busy shift.

sections.h2: What should I check before I give any wait time?
sections.body:
A wait time sounds better when the answer is based on what is actually happening in the restaurant. Before you quote it, check a few basics.

Quick pre-call checklist:

- Current ticket line on the kitchen screen
- Any sold-out items on the menu
- Whether you are taking pickup, delivery, or both
- Whether the caller wants a small order or a large one
- Whether the time is for now or for later

If you use a phone host, keep the menu and hours current so the answer stays accurate. ROAL lets the owner update FAQs, menu items, and hours in the dashboard, and questions it cannot answer land in an inbox. Once you answer one of those questions, the host learns it for next time.

For owners who want to compare options, [the phone answer tools page](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) can help you think through the cost side, while [the FAQ page](/faq) covers common setup questions. The main thing is still the same: give a real number, keep it short, and make the next step easy.

takeaways: Give a range, not a guess, when someone asks how long the wait is.
Use different scripts for pickup, delivery, tables, and after-hours calls.
Base the answer on the current ticket line, not on a hope.
If the call gets complicated, hand it to staff with a summary.
A clear wait time can keep the caller on the line long enough to order.

faq.q: What is the best way to answer “how long is the wait?” on the restaurant phone?
faq.a: Give a short time range and a next step. For example: “We’re about 20 to 25 minutes for pickup right now. I can take your order if you want.” That sounds clear, honest, and useful.

faq.q: Should I give one wait time for all orders?
faq.a: No. Pickup, delivery, and table waits are different, so the estimate should match the type of order or seating request. If the order is large or the restaurant is in a rush, add a buffer and say so plainly.

faq.q: What if I’m too busy to answer every wait time question myself?
faq.a: Use a phone host or a trained script so the answer stays consistent. ROAL can answer common questions, quote a ready time for orders from the live menu, and send the ticket to the kitchen screen.

faq.q: Can I ask the caller to call back later instead of giving a wait time?
faq.a: You can, but it is usually better to give a real estimate and offer a next step. A caller who hears a clear number is more likely to stay on the line than one who only hears “we’re busy.”
